title: Solution Configuration and Buyers Messaging Lab
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview:

This page is a playbook and interactive lab for sales engineers and account teams to:

- Configure an opinionated solution narrative for top buyer personas (Platform/Infra, ML/Product, Security/CISO, Finance).
- Rapidly assemble pricing scenarios and deployment tradeoffs for technical pilots.
- Run a post-demo conversion script and evidence checklist to accelerate procurement.
- Surface short, defensible answers to prospect security questions during qualification calls.

Use this document during pre-demo discovery, demo rehearsals, and pilot-prep workshops. It is intentionally prescriptive — copy the scripts verbatim where helpful and tailor the concrete numbers when a prospect requires bespoke economics.

Purpose and scope:

- Purpose: Reduce friction between demo and pilot contract by providing repeatable messaging, pricing examples, and security evidence.
- Scope: Hosted, Dedicated (reserved capacity), and Private (VPC/on-prem) deployment modes. Includes pricing heuristics for token/embedding economics, reserved commit modeling, and an evidence checklist for common security controls.

Audience:

- Sales Engineers (primary)
- Solutions/Field Engineers
- Account Executives (AE)

Top-line positioning (one-liners by persona):

- Platform/Infra: "Unified inference runtime that turns unpredictable open models into predictable, measurable throughput across regions and tiers."
- ML/Product: "Ship at production scale: consistent latency, KV/prefix caching, and rollout controls so models can be tested and promoted without rewriting serving code."
- Security/CISO: "Deploy in a customer-managed VPC or on-prem with full audit logs, KMS integration, and optional air-gapped packaging."

Persona playbooks (short scripts and evidence nuggets):

1) Platform / Infrastructure Architects
- Pain: Bursty usage, cost unpredictability, noisy neighbors when sharing GPUs.
- Lead with: Dedicated capacity (reserved pools) with autoscaling policies and burst capacity.
- Evidence: Benchmark sheet showing 3 model variants: small (8GB quantized), medium (16GB), large (32+GB) with per-token throughput and P95 latency.
- Script: "We can provision a dedicated pool with pinned-instance-types, baseline throughput of X rps, and a canary policy to shift 10% traffic to a new model for 48 hours before full rollout."

2) ML / Product Managers
- Pain: Model regressions in prod, prompt drift, and subtle quality drops after quantization.
- Lead with: Redwood Optimize suggestions, integrated evals tied to your prompt sets, and safe rollbacks.
- Evidence: Example eval dashboard screenshot and a sample regression alert email.
- Script: "We pair continuous evaluation with automatic fallback: if the new variant drops below your custom metric by >2%, the system reverts to the prior model and sends a trace to your team."

3) Security / Compliance (CISO)
- Pain: Data residency, KMS/HSM controls, auditability.
- Lead with: Private deployment model, customer-controlled KMS keys, and SIEM-compatible audit exports.
- Evidence: SOC2 scope document excerpt, KMS integration guide, sample audit log format (JSON) with fields described.
- Script: "We provide a hardened image for on-prem and a VPC-hosted control-plane with no persistent customer data retention unless configured. We will run the initial integration validation in your staging account."

Competitive brief (talking points vs common alternatives):

- Against big cloud-hosted managed endpoints:
  - Differentiator: Tailored inference optimizations (kernel selection, KV cache) that reduce per-token cost and improve P95 latency versus generic endpoints.
  - Evidence: Internal benchmark highlighting 18–32% cost savings and 20–40% P95 latency improvement on representative LLM workloads.

- Against self-hosting open-source stacks (customer-managed):
  - Differentiator: Faster time-to-production (unified control plane + runbooked upgrades), predictable SLAs, integrated rollout tooling, and cost visibility at token level.
  - Evidence: Migration plan template and a 6-week recommended pilot timeline compared with ~3–6 months for building an in-house serving runtime.

- Against specialized inference vendors:
  - Differentiator: Seamless parity between hosted/dedicated/private modes and built-in eval + cost-optimization toolchain.

Pricing guidance (heuristics & examples):

- Rules of thumb:
  - Hosted: bill per-token generation + per-embedding unit. Typical pilot: 500k–2M tokens/week.
  - Dedicated: monthly reserved capacity priced by GPU-equivalent-hours + moderate per-token surcharge for autoscale bursts.
  - Private: platform fee (one-time) + annual support/maintenance.

- Example scenarios (use these numbers in proposals; adapt by +/- 20%):
  - Early-stage pilot (proof-of-concept) — Hosted
    - Duration: 4–8 weeks
    - Tokens: 1M total
    - Price guidance: $2.5k–$7k (combination of compute and support)
  - Production microservice (mid-market) — Dedicated
    - Baseline commit: 8 GPU-eq months
    - Expected throughput: 300 qps small-size workloads
    - Price guidance: $18k–$40k/month depending on instance types and support SLA
  - Regulated enterprise (on-prem/private)
    - One-time platform fee: $150k–$350k (depends on integration scope)
    - Annual support: 15–25% of platform fee

Conversion playbook: post-demo checklist and 7-step script

1. Recap customer impact: "This demo showed how a 10% latency reduction translates to X fewer server instances and Y% cost reduction per month."
2. Confirm constraints: data residency, SSO, SIEM/alerting needs, contract term.
3. Propose pilot scope: models, workloads, duration, success metrics (latency P95, avg per-token cost, error rate).
4. Share tailored pricing scenario (choose one of the example scenarios above).
5. Evidence pack: SOC2 excerpt, bench spreadsheet, KMS guide, sample SLA language.
6. Arrange technical kickoff within 7 business days and assign a solutions engineer.
7. Close: Suggest a two-step contract (pilot MSA + conversion addendum) to speed procurement.

Pilot success metrics (recommended default SLOs):

- Latency: P95 < 300ms for short-response generation (<=128 tokens) for hosted/dedicated.
- Availability: 99.9% for dedicated pools (SLA-backed).
- Cost: per-token unit cost within 25% of pilot projection after 2 weeks of real traffic.

Security FAQ (short answers for live calls):

Q: Where is customer data stored?
A: For hosted, control-plane metadata is in our managed region; customer payload retention is configurable. For VPC and on-prem, customer data remains in your network.

Q: Do you support customer-managed KMS/HSM?
A: Yes — KMS integration with both cloud KMS (AWS, GCP) and HSM-based key stores for private deployments.

Q: Can you provide audit logs to our SIEM?
A: Yes — structured JSON audit logs with trace IDs, request/response hashes (no plaintext payloads unless allowed), and identity context.

Q: How do you handle model updates and rollbacks?
A: Controlled rollouts, canary percentages, automatic regression detection via integrated evals and automatic fallback policies.

Q: What compliance artefacts do you provide?
A: SOC2 type II summary, penetration test report (redacted), and architecture diagrams for private deployment.

Case study (anonymized, short):

- Customer: Global fintech (anonymous)
- Challenge: Intermittent spikes from chat feature caused 40% latency variance and unpredictable cost.
- Solution: Dedicated GPU pool + KV caching + routing policy.
- Outcome: 28% reduction in P95 latency, 24% reduction in monthly inference cost, and a predictable upgrade path for new model variants.

Appendix: Evidence pack contents (what to attach to proposals)

- Benchmarks spreadsheet (CSV) – latency and throughput for three model variants
- SOC2 executive summary PDF
- KMS integration guide (Markdown)
- Sample SLA wording and data residency annex
- Pilot kickoff checklist (task owners and timelines)

Ownership and next steps:

- Maintenance: Go-to-market owns messaging, Field Engineering owns demo artifacts and bench spreadsheets.
- Update cadence: Quarterly or whenever pricing/benchmarks materially change.
